title: Function Notation, Domain and Range

findings.finding: The mapping examples never isolate the requirement that every element of the stated input set has an output.
findings.breakdown: The rule 'at most one outgoing arrow' classifies every mapping correctly here. The unused input 2 in p7-relation-example does not expose that incomplete rule because input 1 also branches.
findings.checked: Earlier relations teaching permits unused elements of the first set, but does not teach what changes for a function. In p7-identify and p8-q1, every non-function mapping has a branching input; none fails solely because an input has no output. The function example supplies no explicit contrast for this distinction.
findings.assumptions: The displayed left set is the stated input set, as required by the intended outcome's definition of a function.

repair.proposal: After p7-identify-d, add: 'Keep the input and output sets in d unchanged, but erase the arrow from d to 3. Is the resulting relation a function? Explain.' Expected answer: 'No. Input d has no output. Every element of the stated input set must have exactly one output.'

findings.doneWhen: A teaching question explicitly contrasts exactly one output per stated input with an otherwise identical mapping containing an input with no output.

findings.finding: The function-notation topic has no opening review of the binomial expansion, linear equation solving and quadratic factorisation used in its worked examples.
findings.breakdown: Students must expand an algebraic input and solve equations after substituting a specified output. Weak recall of these substantial algebraic methods can prevent them from following the new function-notation decisions.
findings.checked: The preceding functions topic and its exercise practise classification, not expansion or equation solving. Earlier relations teaching rehearses substitution only. The p10 worked examples combine expansion, linear solving and solving a quadratic by factorisation. Taking both square roots occurs in guided practice rather than a worked example, so it is excluded from this finding.
findings.assumptions: These algebraic methods were previously taught in the course's expansion and equation booklets. Ordinary calculator access does not supply the symbolic methods.

repair.proposal: Add three short opening review items: (a) Expand and simplify (x+2)^2+3(x+2). Answer: x^2+7x+10. (b) Solve 3x-4=11. Answer: x=5. (c) Solve x^2-3x-10=0 by factorising. Answer: (x-5)(x+2)=0, so x=5 or x=-2. Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: The opening review rehearses binomial expansion, linear solving and solving a quadratic by factorisation before the p10 examples.

findings.finding: Extend the quadratic function questions by connecting opposite inputs to a shared output and then choosing such an output.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up connects evaluation with finding all inputs for a specified output, using the existing function x^2+1.
findings.checked: For f(x)=x^2+1, f(4)=f(-4)=17 and f(a)=17 gives a=±4. Choosing output 26 gives inputs ±5. Evaluation and solving these equations are available by the end of the topic; no generalisation or enumeration is required.
findings.assumptions: Inputs are real, following the booklet's convention.

repair.proposal: Add optional further parts to p12-q7, stating 'For parts i–m, use f(x)=x^2+1.' (i) Find f(4). Answer: 17. (j) Find f(-4). Answer: 17. (k) Find all a if f(a)=17. Answer: a=±4. (l) Choose a different output greater than 1. Example answer: 26. (m) Find all inputs that give your chosen output. For output 26, answer: ±5.

findings.doneWhen: The optional follow-up asks one question per part and includes expected answers.

findings.finding: Connect the two existing segments and reconsider the domain and range.
findings.breakdown: The added segment fills the gaps in both projections, connecting the graph's continuity across those gaps with its domain and range.
findings.checked: The original segments run from closed (-3,-1) to open (-1,1), and from closed (1,2) to closed (3,3). Adding the closed segment from (-1,1) to (1,2) gives domain [-3,3] and range [-1,3]. The projection and interval methods are already taught.
findings.assumptions: The added segment includes both joining points, making (-1,1) included in the resulting graph.

repair.proposal: Add an optional follow-up to p32-q1-e: 'Add a straight segment joining (-1,1) to (1,2), including both joining points.' (i) What is the domain of the resulting graph? Answer: [-3,3]. (ii) What is its range? Answer: [-1,3].

findings.doneWhen: Both follow-up parts refer to the modified graph and have the stated domain and range.

contextQuestions.question: Have students already learned to interpret the marked vertical and horizontal asymptotes in these graphs, including that the particular branches approach those boundaries without attaining them? The supplied teaching does not explain this, and the other booklet titles do not establish whether it has been taught. If it is new, these tasks need a short explanation before students use the boundaries to exclude inputs or outputs.

protectedGroups.observation: A constant output permits a function, whereas a constant input paired with every real output does not.
protectedGroups.invariant: An ordered-pair description with one fixed coordinate and the other ranging over all real numbers.

protectedGroups.observation: Increasing the lower threshold removes pairs from the relation.
protectedGroups.varies: The added constant in b>a, b>a+1 and b>a+2.
protectedGroups.invariant: The sets A and B, coordinate order and strict comparison.

protectedGroups.invariant: The sets A and B and the direction of comparison.

protectedGroups.varies: Coverage and repetition of first coordinates.
protectedGroups.invariant: The specified sets and valid membership of every coordinate.

protectedGroups.observation: One quadratic rule can give two, one or no real inputs for different specified outputs.

protectedGroups.observation: Subtracting from an output differs from subtracting from an input across different rules.
protectedGroups.invariant: The paired requests f(t)-2 and f(t-2).

protectedGroups.observation: Changing the upper bracket changes only whether the upper endpoint belongs to the interval.
protectedGroups.invariant: Bounds 2 and 4, lower-endpoint inclusion and the offered inequality choices.

protectedGroups.observation: An open endpoint excludes the corresponding boundary values; continuation replaces a finite bound with infinity.
protectedGroups.varies: The lower endpoint changes from closed to open, then the upper endpoint becomes indefinite continuation.
protectedGroups.invariant: Increasing straight graphs with the same lower boundary coordinates; the first two also share the same upper boundary coordinates.

dropped.reason: The existing annotation explicitly identifies f(x) as the output. Thus 2f(-1) applies ordinary multiplication to an already defined numerical output; it does not require an untaught mathematical method. This single added operation does not meet the unsupported-transition threshold, and p15-q19 subsequently tests the input/output distinction explicitly.

candidates.finding: The first operation outside function notation is introduced without explaining that the multiplier acts on the output.
